description: Meghraj Giri is a full stack and frontend developer based in Butwal, Nepal, with five years of production experience. In March 2026 he passed Toptal's screening as a Verified Expert in Engineering.

I have shipped software at five companies — SCSS Consulting, Inseed Tech, Gurzu, Prabidhi Labs and Lightweb Group — after a BSc CSIT at the Institute of Science and Technology, Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu.

Most of that work is transactional, multi-sided product work: marketplaces, clinic and telehealth systems, reservation and resale platforms. Thriftverse is a React Native thrift marketplace with eSewa checkout and Nepal Can Move logistics; Cannabiz Elite is a clinic management system for Australian cannabis and telehealth practices, built on Medusa v2.

The engineering record is measurable. Server-side rendering with Next.js cut initial load time by 30%. A rebuilt admin panel loaded five times faster. A shared component library reduced feature development time by 30–40%. Redesigning Bookvid's onboarding raised user adoption by 35% and retention by 25%.

I work directly with founders and product teams — understanding the core problem, validating the solution, then scaling what works. I take remote projects worldwide from Nepal, usually starting at MVP and staying through production growth.

projects.longDescription: react-weekly-availability-calendar is an MIT-licensed React component published on npm. It renders a weekly grid where a user drags to create an availability slot, then resizes or moves it, with a configurable snap increment of 10, 30 or 60 minutes. Blocked ranges render as a striped, non-interactive overlay. Appearance is controlled three ways — a theme object of CSS variables, per-part class names for Tailwind or plain CSS, or render props for full control of a slot's contents. posts.body:
Search for a developer in Nepal and you get directories — Clutch, GoodFirms, TechBehemoths, Upwork, Twine. They are useful for discovery and close to useless for judgement: listings are self-submitted, ranking is influenced by paid placement, and a five-star average across four reviews tells you very little.

This is a guide to the judgement part.

## Where Nepali developers actually are

Nepal's software industry is concentrated in **Kathmandu**, with a smaller and growing base in **Pokhara**, **Butwal** and **Chitwan**. The larger firms — Leapfrog, Verisk, Cotiviti — employ hundreds of engineers and mostly serve overseas clients. Below them sit dozens of agencies of ten to fifty people, and below those a large independent population working through Upwork, Toptal, Truelancer and direct referral.

Where someone sits in that stack changes what you get:

- **Large firms** are for multi-year engagements with a team and a contract to match. They will not take a six-week MVP.
- **Small agencies** give you a project manager and continuity if someone leaves. You pay for that layer, and the person you brief is usually not the person writing the code.
- **Independents** give you directness and lower cost with no bus factor. Right for a defined scope, wrong for something that needs four people in parallel.

## What to actually check

**Look at code, not a portfolio grid.** A screenshot proves a designer was involved. Ask for a GitHub profile and read a repository — commit history tells you whether someone works steadily or in panicked bursts before deadlines.

**Ask what broke.** Any developer can describe a project that went well. The useful question is what went wrong, what they would do differently, and what they cut from v1. Someone who cannot answer specifically has either not shipped much or was not close to the decisions.

**Prefer credentials someone else issued.** A self-described "senior developer" means nothing. Screening from Toptal or Arc, a degree from a named institution, and named employers with dates are all things a third party had to agree to.

**Check the overlap, not the timezone.** Nepal runs on UTC+5:45. That is a full working-day overlap with Australia, India and Southeast Asia, a morning overlap with Europe, and for the United States a scheduled window rather than live afternoon hours. If your team does everything synchronously, that last one matters more than any rate difference.

**Insist on a written scope before money moves.** The single most common failure in small engagements is not incompetence, it is two people who believed they had agreed on different things.

## What it costs

Rates in Nepal sit well below Australia, the United States and Western Europe, which is why so many teams look here in the first place. Independent rates vary widely by experience and by whether you are hiring through a marketplace that takes a cut.

Be careful reading rate as a proxy for quality in either direction. The cheapest quote usually reflects someone who has not understood the scope, and will surface as change requests later. The most expensive is not automatically the most capable.

Ask for a project quote after a scope conversation rather than an hourly rate. The same feature can take a week or a month depending on what it must integrate with, and an hourly number quoted before that conversation is a guess wearing a suit.

## The honest summary

There is no ranked list of "the best developers in Nepal" worth trusting, including this article — the directories that publish them are ranking by who paid or who submitted, not by who ships. What you can do is check evidence you can inspect: public code, named employers, third-party screening, and a specific answer about something that went wrong.

I am one of the independents described above — a full stack developer in Butwal with five years of production work, seven published case studies, and Toptal Verified Expert status since March 2026. If that fits what you are building, [the case studies are here](/projects) and [my background is here](/about).

posts.body:
Most articles on this answer with a range and stop. A range is nearly useless on its own, because the same feature can cost four times as much depending on details that have nothing to do with anyone's hourly rate.

Here is what actually moves the number.

## Hourly rate is the least informative part

A rate multiplied by a guess is a guess. Two developers quoting the same hourly figure can differ by a factor of three on the same brief, because one has built the thing before and one is learning on your budget.

What compresses the estimate is specificity: a written scope, a decision about what is *not* in v1, and clarity on what the software has to integrate with.

## What actually drives cost

**Integrations.** A checkout is a week. A checkout wired into eSewa or Khalti, with a logistics provider on the other side and reconciliation when a payment succeeds but a delivery fails, is not a week. Every external system you touch adds its own failure modes.

**Regulatory surface.** Ordinary software has bugs; regulated software has obligations. Healthcare, payments and anything holding identity documents carry audit trails, consent handling and data-residency rules that shape the data model from day one.

**Mobile versus web.** A mobile app carries app-store review, release management, device fragmentation and a release cycle you do not control. Budget for the release process, not only the build.

**Design state.** Finished Figma files with defined states are cheapest to build from. "We'll figure out the design as we go" is the single most reliable way to double a front-end estimate.

**Who maintains it.** A quote to build is not a quote to run. Ask explicitly what happens after launch and who fixes the thing that breaks in month three.

## Marketplace fees

Hiring through Upwork, Toptal, Truelancer or Fiverr adds a platform margin — sometimes on the freelancer's side, sometimes yours, often both. You are buying escrow, dispute resolution and vetting, which are genuinely worth something on a first engagement with a stranger.

Direct engagement removes that margin and the protection with it. It makes sense once trust is established, or when you can verify someone independently through public code and named references.

## The costs that show up later

- **Scope drift.** The commonest overrun, and it is rarely anyone's fault — it is what happens when nobody writes down what "done" means.
- **Handover.** Undocumented code costs the next developer weeks. Ask for a README and a runbook as deliverables, in the contract.
- **Infrastructure.** Hosting, managed databases, email, SMS, error tracking. Small monthly amounts that nobody includes in the build quote.
- **The second platform.** "We'll add iOS later" is not a small addition unless it was designed for from the start.

## How to ask for a number

Give the developer four things: what the product does, who it is for, what it must integrate with, and any fixed deadline. Ask for a project quote with the assumptions written down, and ask what is deliberately excluded.

If a quote arrives without stated assumptions, it is not an estimate. It is a hope.

If you want to test this: [describe what you are building](/contact) and you will get a scope conversation before any number.

posts.body:
Nepal's software industry gets written about as though it were only Kathmandu. Most of it is. But the part of the job that requires being in Kathmandu has been shrinking for years, and I have spent five of them building software from **Butwal**, in Lumbini Province, about 250 km west of the capital.

## Why this works now and did not before

Three things changed. Fibre reached the mid-west, so a video call is no longer a negotiation with the connection. Payment rails — Wise, Payoneer, the marketplaces — made getting paid from abroad ordinary rather than an ordeal. And the industry stopped treating remote work as a concession.

The result is that the constraint on working from a smaller city is no longer infrastructure. It is proximity to other developers, which is a real cost and worth naming.

## The timezone maths

Nepal runs on **UTC+5:45**, one of the very few 45-minute offsets in the world. Practically:

- **Australia**: two to four hours ahead. A full overlapping working day. Most of my recent work has been for Australian clients, and this is why.
- **India and Southeast Asia**: near-identical hours.
- **Europe**: my afternoon is their morning. Comfortable for a daily sync.
- **United States**: no natural overlap. It works on a scheduled window and asynchronous written updates, and it works badly if a team insists on doing everything in meetings.

That last point is the honest limitation. If your team runs on live conversation, a 10-to-12-hour offset is a real cost, and no amount of goodwill removes it.

## What the work has looked like

The projects have not been small-town projects. A clinic management system for Australian cannabis and telehealth practices, built on Medusa v2 with a prescription portal integrated. A thrift marketplace shipped to iOS and Android with eSewa checkout and Nepal Can Move handling delivery. An inventory system built as an installable progressive web app so it keeps working when the connection does not — a requirement that comes from actually living somewhere the connection sometimes does not.

That last one is worth dwelling on. Building from Butwal makes you take offline-first, low-bandwidth and flaky-network cases seriously, because you experience them. Developers on reliable connections tend to treat those as edge cases. For a large share of the world's users they are the normal case.

## On the local scene

Butwal has a growing number of developers and a handful of small agencies, and Tribhuvan University's affiliated colleges here produce a steady stream of CSIT graduates. What it does not have is the density of Kathmandu — fewer meetups, fewer people to ask, a smaller pool for hiring into a team.

I have handled that the way most people outside a capital do: online communities, open source, and staying deliberately in touch with people I have worked with. It is a workable substitute. It is not the same thing, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.

## If you are hiring from here

The questions worth asking a developer outside Kathmandu are the same ones worth asking any remote developer: can I see the code, who has verified them, what does their overlap with my team actually look like, and what happened on a project that went wrong.

My answers are on [my background](/about) and in the [case studies](/projects), and you can [start a conversation here](/contact).

posts.description: What it is like building software for international clients from Butwal, Nepal — timezone overlap, the local developer scene outside Kathmandu, and how remote work actually runs from Lumbini Province.
